title: Acidity & Heartburn (Amlapitta): Ayurvedic Causes, Diet & Daily Routine
excerpt: Burning in the chest, sour belching and heaviness in the stomach — acidity is a problem in almost every home today. Learn how Ayurveda understands Amlapitta — causes, symptoms, what to eat and avoid, daily routine, yoga, safe home remedies and when you must see a doctor immediately.
content:
Burning in the chest after meals, sour fluid rising up to the throat, frequent sour belching or a bloated stomach — such complaints are very common today. Late-night dinners, tea and coffee, fried and spicy food, stress and too little sleep are major causes. Many people manage by taking an antacid or tablet every day, but do not pay attention to the real cause.

In Ayurveda this problem is called Amlapitta. The good news is that in most people the right diet, meals on time and a balanced daily routine can bring considerable relief. This article is for information only — take treatment only on the advice of your Vaidya or doctor.

What is acidity?

Our stomach makes acid to digest food. Between the stomach and the food pipe (oesophagus) there is a valve-like muscle that stops this acid from coming up. When too much acid is made or this valve becomes loose, acid starts rising into the food pipe and causes burning in the chest (heartburn).

Occasional acidity is common. But if it happens two or more times a week regularly, it is called GERD (Gastro-Oesophageal Reflux Disease), which needs investigation and regular care. If ignored for a long time, it can lead to inflammation of the food pipe, ulcers or other problems.

The Ayurvedic view: Amlapitta

According to Ayurveda, Amlapitta mainly arises from aggravation of Pitta dosha and weakness of Agni (digestive fire). Madhava Nidana describes its cause as follows:

विरुद्धदुष्टाम्लविदाहिपित्तप्रकोपिपानान्नभुजो विदग्धम् ।
पित्तं स्वहेतूपचितं पुरा यत् तदम्लपित्तं प्रवदन्ति सन्तः ॥
— Madhava Nidana, Amlapitta Nidana (Chapter 51)

Meaning: In a person who eats and drinks incompatible, spoiled (stale), very sour, burning and Pitta-aggravating food, the Pitta that has already accumulated from its own causes becomes vidagdha (improperly digested and sour) — this is what the learned call Amlapitta.

In simple words, when Agni is weak, food is not digested properly, sourness (vidaha) develops, and Pitta, whose nature is hot and sharp, increases further. Kapha and Vata can also be involved: with Kapha there is more heaviness, nausea and loss of appetite; with Vata there is more bloating and pain.

Main causes of acidity

  • Very spicy, fried, sour food with too much salt and chilli
  • No fixed meal times, staying hungry, or snacking again and again
  • Eating late at night and lying down or sleeping right after meals
  • Too much tea, coffee, cold drinks, alcohol and smoking/tobacco
  • Incompatible food (viruddha ahara) — such as milk with sour fruits, salty snacks or fish
  • Stress, anger, worry and staying awake late at night
  • Taking painkillers without a doctor's advice or on an empty stomach
  • Obesity (especially belly fat), pregnancy and very tight clothes

Symptoms

  • Burning in the chest or upper abdomen
  • Sour or bitter belching, sour fluid rising to the throat
  • Heaviness, bloating or nausea
  • Mouth ulcers or a bitter taste in the mouth
  • Low appetite or discomfort after eating
  • Cough, sore throat or hoarse voice when lying down at night
  • Sometimes headache, dizziness or tiredness

Remember — chest pain or burning is not always acidity. If the pain comes with sweating, breathlessness, or spreads to the left arm, jaw or back, it may be a heart problem — go to a hospital immediately.

Tests

Ordinary acidity often does not need tests. But if the complaint keeps coming back, does not improve even with medicine, or there are danger signs, the doctor may advise these tests:

  • Endoscopy — examination of the inside of the food pipe and stomach
  • Test for H. pylori — this bacterium is a common cause of stomach inflammation and ulcers
  • Blood test (such as haemoglobin) — to detect anaemia

Diet: what to eat, what to avoid

In Amlapitta, diet is the biggest medicine. Light, easily digestible food with a cooling nature calms Pitta.

What to eat

  • Grains: old rice, barley, wheat roti, daliya (broken wheat)
  • Pulses: moong dal, masoor — with little chilli and spice
  • Vegetables: bottle gourd (lauki), ridge gourd, pointed gourd (parwal), tinda, pumpkin, ash gourd (petha), cucumber
  • Fruits: ripe banana, papaya, pomegranate, pear, sweet apple, amla
  • Drinks: coconut water, fennel (saunf) or coriander water, lukewarm or plain water
  • A little desi ghee (in food) — considered helpful in calming Pitta
  • Chewing a little fennel after meals

What to avoid or greatly reduce

  • Green chilli, red chilli, garam masala, pickles and chutneys
  • Samosa, pakoras, puri, fast food and things made of maida
  • Sour curd, tamarind, tomato and sour fruits in large amounts
  • Tea, coffee, cold drinks, soda and alcohol
  • Chocolate, very sweet foods and bakery items
  • Stale, repeatedly reheated food, or very cold food straight from the fridge
  • Tea or painkillers on an empty stomach

The right way to eat

Eat at a fixed time every day, with a calm mind, slowly and chewing well. Eat a little less than your hunger — leave part of the stomach empty. Do not stay hungry for long, because acid troubles an empty stomach too. Dinner should be light and at least 2–3 hours before sleeping.

Daily routine, yoga and pranayama

  • Wake up early in the morning and sleep on time at night (by about 10 PM)
  • Do not lie down right after eating; walk slowly for 10–15 minutes
  • If acidity is worse at night, keep the head end of the bed slightly raised and sleep on your left side
  • Do not wear very tight belts or clothes around the waist
  • If overweight, reduce weight gradually
  • Avoid working long in the sun and getting very angry — these increase Pitta
  • Completely give up smoking, tobacco and alcohol

Yoga and pranayama

  • Asanas: Vajrasana (5–10 minutes after meals), Sukhasana, Balasana, Setu Bandhasana, Shavasana
  • Pranayama: Anulom-Vilom, Bhramari, Sheetali and Sheetkari (at a gentle pace)

Apart from Vajrasana, do yoga only on an empty stomach or 3–4 hours after a meal. During acidity, avoid Kapalbhati, deep forward bends and inverted poses. Learn yoga from a trained teacher; if you have heart disease, high BP, pregnancy, hernia or a recent operation, ask your Vaidya/doctor first. Do not do Sheetali or Sheetkari if you have asthma or a cold.

Safe home remedies

  • Fennel (saunf): chew a little fennel after meals, or drink water of fennel soaked overnight in the morning
  • Coriander water: soak whole coriander seeds in water at night, strain and drink in the morning
  • Coconut water: once a day, especially in summer
  • Amla: fresh amla or amla juice (diluted with water) — considered Pitta-calming
  • Fresh ash gourd (petha) or bottle gourd juice: in a small amount; if it tastes bitter, do not drink it at all

These remedies can give relief in mild and occasional acidity. Patients with diabetes or kidney disease should ask their doctor before taking coconut water and fruit juices. If there is no relief within 1–2 weeks, do not rely on home remedies alone — get tested.

Ayurvedic herbs — with caution

Ayurvedic texts mention many Pitta-calming medicines for Amlapitta, such as Yashtimadhu (liquorice/mulethi), Amalaki (amla), Shatavari, Guduchi (giloy), Dhanyaka (coriander), Patola and classical formulations like Avipattikar Churna. However:

  • Which medicine, in what dose and for how long — the Vaidya decides this only after looking at each person's prakriti, pulse, age and stage of the disease.
  • Taking liquorice (mulethi) for a long time or in large amounts can raise BP; patients with high BP, heart or kidney disease and pregnant women should not take it without a Vaidya's advice.
  • Do not stop your ongoing acidity medicine on your own. If you have been taking an acidity tablet daily for a long time, decide about reducing or changing it only together with your doctor.
  • In pregnancy, breastfeeding, children and the elderly, give any herb only on the advice of a Vaidya/doctor. Beware of claims like “acidity removed from the root”.

When to see a doctor immediately

  • Chest pain with sweating, breathlessness or pain spreading to the arm/jaw — go to hospital immediately
  • Difficulty or pain in swallowing food or water
  • Vomiting blood, coffee-coloured vomit, or black sticky stools
  • Unexplained weight loss, loss of appetite or anaemia
  • Repeated vomiting or severe stomach pain
  • Acidity starting for the first time after the age of 50, or complaints lasting more than 2 weeks despite medicine

Summary — points to remember

  • Meals on time, light and well chewed; early dinner
  • Reduce or stop chilli-spice, fried food, tea-coffee and alcohol
  • Do not lie down after eating; sleep well and reduce stress
  • Do not stop ongoing medicines on your own; see a doctor at once for danger signs
  • Ayurvedic treatment only on the advice of an experienced Vaidya
